question: How does Stellar differ from the XRP Ledger in consensus, transaction fees, and how assets are issued?

golden.answer: In the Stellar Consensus Protocol (SCP), each validator chooses its own quorum set; XRP Ledger servers each trust a Unique Node List. Stellar launched in 2014 on Ripple-derived code and switched to SCP in 2015. Stellar sends fees to a locked account no one can spend; the XRP Ledger destroys them. On Stellar every asset but XLM has an issuer, and holders opt in with a trustline; XRP Ledger tokens also use trust lines.
keyFacts: In Stellar's SCP, each validator chooses its own quorum set.
Stellar replaced its original Ripple-derived consensus with SCP in 2015.
Stellar transaction fees go to a locked account that no one can spend.
Stellar classic assets have an issuer, and holders opt in with a trustline.
avoid: Do NOT say Stellar still runs the Ripple or XRP Ledger consensus protocol.
golden.notes: XRP Ledger properties (Unique Node List, destroyed fees, trust-line tokens) are context an answer may attribute to the XRP Ledger; they are not required. A false XRP Ledger claim is still wrong. Mentioning XRP Ledger Multi-Purpose Tokens or Stellar contract tokens alongside trust lines is correct, not required.

sources.quote: The Stellar network reaches consensus using the Stellar Consensus Protocol (SCP), which is a construction of the Federated Byzantine Agree[ment]
A unique node list (UNL) is a server's list of validators that it trusts not to collude. Every XRP Ledger server is configured with a UNL
All transactions included in a ledger destroy some XRP as a transaction cost
The lumens collected from transaction fees go into a locked account and are not given to or used by anyone.
Anyone can issue trust line tokens by sending a Payment transaction if the necessary trust lines are in place.
The lumen is the only token that doesn't require an issuer or trustline.
Stellar started in 2014 on code from the XRP Ledger and switched to its own Stellar Consensus Protocol in 2015.

corroboration.claim: Stellar uses SCP, a federated Byzantine agreement protocol in which each node sets its own quorum set; the XRP Ledger has each server trust a Unique Node List.

evidence.note: 'A node's opinion on a statement depends on the opinions of its quorum set.'
Every XRP Ledger server is configured with a UNL.
Comparison table: XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol (validator UNLs) versus Stellar Consensus Protocol (federated Byzantine agreement).

corroboration.claim: XRP Ledger transaction costs are destroyed; Stellar fees go to a locked fee pool that no account can spend.

evidence.note: 'Every transaction must specify how much XRP to destroy to pay the transaction cost.'
Fees 'go into a locked account and are not given to or used by anyone'.
'XRP Ledger fees are destroyed, while Stellar fees go into a locked account that no one uses.'

corroboration.claim: Both networks issue non-native assets through trust lines to an issuer.

evidence.note: Trust line tokens: the side with the negative balance is the issuer.
Every asset except the lumen requires an issuer and a trustline.
'both support issued assets and on-ledger trading'.

corroboration.claim: Stellar launched in 2014 on Ripple-derived code and replaced its consensus with SCP in 2015.

Current docs describe SCP as the network's consensus protocol.

corroboration.claim: The upgraded Stellar network running the Stellar Consensus Protocol went live on 2015-11-03.

evidence.note: Post dated 2015-11-03: 'The upgraded Stellar network is here! ... It uses the Stellar Consensus Protocol (SCP)'; the code is 'less than half the size of the previous codebase'.

corroboration.claim: Every Stellar asset except the lumen has an issuer, and an account opts in to hold it with a trustline.

evidence.note: 'Trustlines are an explicit opt-in for an account to hold a particular asset. To hold a specific asset, an account must establish a trustline with the issuing account'.
